extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning proofs / discrete mathematics (readers of 'Book of Proof')
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions and criteria for relations on sets (reflexive, symmetric, transitive), equivalence relations, equivalence classes, and partitions, together with visual/technical tests and proof techniques used to verify these properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a relation
rubrics_metrics.description: A relation on a set A is a subset R ⊆ A × A. We often abbreviate the statement (x,y) ∈ R as xRy. The statement (x,y) ∉ R is abbreviated as xR y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret relations as sets of ordered pairs; any subset of A×A (including arbitrary or 'meaningless' subsets) is a relation. Use set-builder notation for infinite relations and diagrams (arrows) for visualization when feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflexive
rubrics_metrics.description: Relation R is reflexive if xRx for every x ∈ A. That is, R is reflexive if ∀x ∈ A, xRx.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spotting criterion in diagrams: there is a loop at every point x. Examples: =, |, and ≤ are reflexive on suitable domains. Non-examples: <, >, ≠ are not reflexive. To prove reflexivity, show the defining property holds for an arbitrary element (e.g., for = (mod n) observe n|(x−x)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Symmetric
rubrics_metrics.description: Relation R is symmetric if xRy implies yRx for all x,y ∈ A. That is, R is symmetric if ∀x,y ∈ A, xRy → yRx.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spotting criterion in diagrams: whenever there is an arrow from x to y there is an arrow back from y to x. Examples: equality (=) and 'same parity as' relations are symmetric. Non-examples: < is not symmetric. To prove symmetry use a direct proof assuming xRy and deducing yRx (e.g., for congruence modulo n, multiply by −1 to get the reverse divisibility).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitive
rubrics_metrics.description: Relation R is transitive if whenever xRy and yRz, then also xRz. That is, R is transitive if ∀x,y,z ∈ A, ((xRy) ∧ (yRz)) → xRz.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spotting criterion in diagrams: whenever there are arrows x→y and y→z, there must be an arrow x→z. Note special cases (if x=z, transitivity typically implies a loop at x when xRy and yRx). Examples: <, =, and divisibility (|) are transitive. Prove transitivity by assuming xRy and yRz and deducing xRz (for congruence mod n add the two divisibility equalities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual tests for relation properties (diagram heuristics)
rubrics_metrics.description: How to spot reflexive, symmetric and transitive properties from relation diagrams: reflexive → loop at every point; symmetric → for every arrow x→y there is an arrow y→x back; transitive → whenever arrows x→y and y→z exist there is an arrow x→z.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use diagrams to quickly identify failures (e.g., missing loop shows non-reflexive). Diagrams are limited for large or infinite relations; use formal proofs in those cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence relation
rubrics_metrics.description: A relation R on a set A is an equivalence relation if it is reflexive, symmetric and transitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalence relations express a notion of 'sameness' (equality or a weaker notion). They occur frequently in mathematics; once verified, treat the relation as partitioning the set into classes. Typical examples: equality, congruence modulo n, 'same parity', 'same degree' (for polynomials).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence class
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an equivalence relation R on A and any element a ∈ A, the equivalence class containing a is the subset [a] = { x ∈ A : xRa }.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalence classes collect all elements 'the same as' a. Use set notation to describe classes (e.g., for degree-of-polynomial relation, [3x^2+2] = {ax^2+bx+c : a ≠ 0}).

rubrics_metrics.name: [a] = [b] iff aRb (characterization of equality of classes)
rubrics_metrics.description: For an equivalence relation R on A and a,b ∈ A, [a] = [b] if and only if aRb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is Theorem 11.1; the proof depends on reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity. Use this criterion to check when two equivalence classes coincide and to move between membership in classes and pairwise relation statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence classes form a partition
rubrics_metrics.description: The set of equivalence classes of an equivalence relation R on A is a partition of A: the classes are non-empty, their union equals A, and distinct classes are disjoint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the partition viewpoint to reason about grouping of elements (e.g., congruence mod n yields the partition {[0],[1],...,[n−1]}).

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting equivalence classes for congruence mod n
rubrics_metrics.description: The equivalence relation = (mod n) on Z has exactly n equivalence classes [0],[1],...,[n−1].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct classes by remainders; show every integer belongs to exactly one class. Use this as a model for finite index equivalence relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof techniques for relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Common proof methods illustrated: direct proof (assume relation instance and derive the consequence), algebraic manipulation for arithmetic/divisibility relations, use of set notation and element-chasing for class equality and partition proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: to show = (mod n) is symmetric, assume n|(x−y) and multiply by −1 to get n|(y−x); to show transitivity, add n|(x−y) and n|(y−z) to get n|(x−z). For class equality use element-wise subset arguments (show [a] ⊆ [b] and [b] ⊆ [a]).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relations may be arbitrary subsets (no required 'meaning')
rubrics_metrics.description: Any subset R of A×A is a relation on A, whether or not it describes anything familiar or meaningful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even 'random' subsets are valid relations; when no intuitive meaning exists, treat R formally as a set of pairs and analyze properties via the defining membership condition.
